title: Integrating LLM with Existing Infrastructure
author: shashank ms
summary: Integrating a large language model into production infrastructure rarely starts with a blank slate. Most engineering teams already run REST APIs, microservices, queue workers, and observability stacks. The goal is not to rebuild around the LLM, but to treat it as another inference dependency that slots into existing patterns for routing, retries, cost control, and monitoring. This guide covers practical patterns for wiring an LLM provider into your current architecture without fragmenting your stack. SDK Compatibility and Drop-In Migration If your services already use the OpenAI Python or Node.js SDK, adopting Oxlo.ai is a configuration change, not a refactor. Point the base URL to https://api.oxlo.ai/v1 , swap the API key, and keep your existing Pydantic models, streaming parsers, and error handling logic. import os import openai client = openai.OpenAI( base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key=os.environ["OXLO_API_KEY"] ) response = client.chat.completions.create( model="llama-3.3-70b", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize the attached logs."}], stream=True ) Because Oxlo.ai returns standard chat completion shapes, your existing middleware for JSON mode, function calling, and vision inputs continues to work without branching logic. API Gateway and Proxy Patterns Production systems rarely expose LLM keys to client applications. Instead, traffic flows through an API gateway or sidecar that manages authentication, rate limiting, and request transformation. You can add Oxlo.ai as an upstream provider in nginx, Envoy, or a custom FastAPI proxy. A minimal FastAPI gateway route might look like this: from fastapi import FastAPI, Request import httpx app = FastAPI() OXLO_BASE = "https://api.oxlo.ai/v1" @app.post("/v1/chat/completions") async def proxy_chat(request: Request): body = await request.json() async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client: r = await client.post( f"{OXLO_BASE}/chat/completions", headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {OXLO_API_KEY}"}, json=body, timeout=60.0 ) return r.json() Because Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing rather than token-based metering, your gateway does not need a token counting sidecar to estimate costs before forwarding large prompts. This simplifies request flow for agentic workloads and long-context pipelines. Routing, Failovers, and Load Balancing Multi-provider setups are common for risk mitigation. A routing layer can send standard queries to one provider and fall back to Oxlo.ai for workloads where predictable billing or model availability matters. Oxlo.ai offers no cold starts on popular models, so your health checks and timeout budgets do not need to account for warm-up latency. Here is a simple Python retry wrapper: import openai clients = { "oxlo.ai": openai.OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key=OXLO_KEY), "backup": openai.OpenAI(base_url="https://backup.example.com/v1", api_key=BACKUP_KEY), } def chat_with_fallback(model: str, messages: list): for name, client in clients.items(): try: return client.chat.completions.create(model=model, messages=messages) except Exception: continue raise RuntimeError("All providers exhausted") This pattern keeps your infrastructure resilient without introducing provider-specific SDKs. Cost Predictability with Request-Based Pricing Token-based billing complicates infrastructure integration because costs scale with input length. When an LLM sits behind a queue worker or data pipeline, prompt sizes can vary by orders of magnitude, making budgets unpredictable. Oxlo.ai charges a flat rate per API request regardless of prompt length, which means your existing cost allocation tags, per-endpoint budgets, and usage alarms can treat LLM calls like fixed-price API dependencies. For long-context retrieval pipelines or agent loops that send large prompts repeatedly, this model aligns costs with business actions rather than token volume. Teams running workloads against token-based providers such as Together AI, Fireworks AI, OpenRouter, Replicate, or Anyscale often find that Oxlo.ai request-based pricing becomes significantly cheaper for long-context workloads. See https://oxlo.ai/pricing for current plan details. Observability and Structured Logging Integrating an LLM into existing infrastructure means fitting it into your current logging and tracing standards. Because Oxlo.ai returns standard OpenAI-compatible response shapes, you can reuse existing parsers for streaming chunks, function calls, and tool outputs. When logging, structure your records to capture model name, request ID, latency, and business context. If you run distributed traces, tag spans with the provider endpoint so you can compare Oxlo.ai against other routes in your stack. Standard HTTP status codes and JSON error bodies mean your existing alerting rules for 5xx rates or latency thresholds apply without custom mapping. Security and Access Control Treat your LLM API key like any other service secret. Store it in your existing secret manager, rotate it through your standard cycle, and scope permissions by environment. Oxlo.ai provides standard HTTP Bearer authentication, so your API gateway or service mesh can attach headers without custom plugins. If you segment networks by workload sensitivity, you can route traffic through private egress gateways. Oxlo.ai is accessible via standard HTTPS on https://api.oxlo.ai/v1 , which integrates cleanly with corporate proxies and VPC outbound rules. Putting It Together Integrating an LLM should feel like adding a high-performance microservice, not adopting a monolith. By leveraging OpenAI SDK compatibility, request-based pricing, and standard REST semantics, Oxlo.ai drops into existing infrastructure with minimal friction. Whether you are routing through an API gateway, managing multi-provider fallbacks, or controlling costs for variable-length workloads, Oxlo.ai provides a predictable, developer-first layer that respects the architecture you already have.

title: Why I Don’t Want AI Coding Agents to Have Shell Access by Default
author: Lucas
summary: AI coding agents are becoming very good at working with real codebases. They can inspect a repository, trace bugs across multiple files, suggest architectural changes, write tests, and increasingly implement entire features. But there is a security question I think we are moving past too quickly: How much access does an AI actually need to do useful work? When I want an AI model to review my code, I usually want it to do things like: understand the project structure; read source files; search for symbols or patterns; trace how components interact; identify bugs; review a proposed implementation. None of those tasks inherently require unrestricted shell access. Yet many agent workflows bundle code access together with capabilities such as: executing shell commands; running Git; launching processes; reading arbitrary filesystem locations; modifying arbitrary files. That makes the agent much more capable. It also dramatically increases the blast radius when something goes wrong. Capability and access are different things A stronger model does not necessarily need stronger permissions. Suppose I ask an AI: Review the authentication implementation and tell me if you see any security issues. For that task, the model needs information. It needs to read the relevant repository. It probably does not need permission to: run arbitrary commands read my entire home directory inspect unrelated projects modify source files access credentials delete files This seems obvious when written out. But developer tooling often treats repository access and machine access as almost the same thing. I wanted to separate them. The principle: least privilege Traditional security engineering has a simple idea: Give a system only the permissions it needs to perform its job. AI agents should not be an exception. If I am using one model as a reviewer, its permissions should reflect the role of a reviewer. That might mean: ✓ list repository files ✓ read approved files ✓ search the repository ✗ execute shell commands ✗ run Git ✗ launch processes ✗ read outside the repository ✗ arbitrarily modify source code This doesn't eliminate every risk. But it turns the question from: "Do I trust this AI with my computer?" into something much narrower: "Do I trust this AI to inspect this repository through these specific operations?" That is a much easier security boundary to reason about. This is why I built RepoRelay I recently built an open-source project called RepoRelay around this idea. RepoRelay is an MCP server that sits between an AI client and a local repository. The architecture is roughly: AI / ChatGPT ↓ Secure MCP connection ↓ RepoRelay ↓ one explicitly approved repository Instead of exposing a general-purpose shell or filesystem API, RepoRelay exposes a deliberately small set of repository operations. The read-only surface is essentially: open_workspace list_files read_file search_files The important part isn't the number of tools. It's what isn't there. There is no shell tool. There is no Git tool. There is no process-execution tool. There is no generic "write this file anywhere" tool. The approved repository becomes the boundary. "One repository" sounds simple. It isn't. A security boundary based on filesystem paths has plenty of edge cases. Checking that a requested path starts with: C:\Projects\my-app is nowhere near sufficient. A tool like this has to think about things such as: .. traversal; absolute paths; path canonicalization; symbolic links; junctions and reparse points; hard links; sensitive files; hidden credential locations; bounded reads and searches. For example, a request for: ../../some-other-project/.env should obviously fail. But the less-obvious escape mechanisms matter just as much. RepoRelay therefore treats containment as an enforced security property rather than a prompt instruction. The AI isn't being told: "Please stay inside this folder." The server is supposed to make leaving the folder impossible through the tools it exposes. That distinction is important. Sensitive files deserve another boundary Even inside an approved repository, there are files I usually don't want an AI reviewer reading. The most obvious example is: .env A repository may also contain credentials, private keys, or other sensitive material. So "the AI may read this repository" should not automatically mean: "The AI may read every byte under this directory." RepoRelay blocks classes of sensitive paths separately from the repository-root boundary. That gives you two layers: Is this inside the approved repository? ↓ yes ↓ Is this file allowed to be exposed? ↓ yes ↓ read Again, none of this is revolutionary security theory. It's applying established ideas to AI tooling. Reviewer and implementer should not always be the same agent This led me to another design decision. I often use one AI system to implement code and a stronger model to review the result. Those are different roles. The implementer may genuinely need local execution capabilities: edit code run tests compile use Git The reviewer often doesn't. So instead of giving both agents identical privileges, I prefer a workflow like: Local coding agent ↓ implements change ↓ repository / commit ↓ RepoRelay ↓ strong reviewer model ↓ review This also creates a useful separation of concerns. The model that wrote the code isn't necessarily the model that decides the code is good. But what if the reviewer needs to request changes? Pure read-only access is the cleanest security model, and RepoRelay supports it. But I also wanted to experiment with a constrained reviewer → implementer workflow. Instead of allowing arbitrary writes, RepoRelay can expose a few predetermined handoff files. Conceptually: ChatGPT ↓ NEXT_TASK.md local coding agent ↓ implements changes ↓ RESULT.md ChatGPT ↓ REVIEW.md The reviewer can communicate what should happen next without gaining generic write access to the source tree. That's a very different permission from: "Edit whatever file you want." The goal is not zero capability. The goal is bounded capability. Why not just use operating-system permissions? OS-level isolation is valuable, and a tool like RepoRelay is not a replacement for containers, VMs, sandboxing, or proper system permissions. Those solve a broader problem. RepoRelay is trying to solve a narrower one at the application layer: What operations should this particular AI client be able to invoke? Those layers can complement each other. You might eventually have: OS / container sandbox + MCP-level capability restrictions + repository containment + sensitive-file filtering Security tends to work better when it does not depend on a single control. What RepoRelay does not claim I think security-oriented projects should be explicit about their limitations. RepoRelay is not an operating-system sandbox. If malicious software is already running under your user account, an MCP server cannot magically secure the rest of the machine from that software. It also doesn't make AI-generated code safe. A reviewer can still miss vulnerabilities. The purpose is narrower: Reduce the authority granted to the AI connection itself. That still matters. If the task requires reading four source files, giving the model the ability to execute arbitrary commands is unnecessary additional authority. AI tooling needs better permission design As models improve, I think permission design is going to matter more, not less. A weak model with powerful permissions is dangerous because it can make mistakes. A very capable model with powerful permissions deserves careful thought for a different reason: it can do much more. The answer can't simply be: "The model is smarter now, so give it everything." We should be asking: What is the smallest useful interface for this task? For code review, that interface can be surprisingly small. And once the permissions are explicit, they become much easier to inspect, test, audit, and reason about. RepoRelay is open source RepoRelay is still a very new project, and I'm actively working on the security model and developer experience. It's MIT licensed and available on GitHub: github.com/Lukie-81/RepoRelay You can install it through npm: npm install -g reporelay-mcp@latest I'm especially interested in feedback from people working on MCP, agent security, local-first tooling, and coding-agent workflows. I'm sure there are threat-model assumptions and edge cases I haven't considered yet. That's also part of why I wanted to make it open source. The broader question is bigger than RepoRelay: When an AI only needs access to your code, why should we automatically give it access to your machine?

title: Best Strategy Frameworks Every Product Leader Should Know
author: David Weaver
summary: Product leaders have no shortage of frameworks. There are frameworks for prioritization, discovery, roadmapping, growth, pricing, positioning, customer interviews, experimentation, and almost every other activity that happens inside a product organization. Strategy is different. A prioritization framework can help decide whether Feature A should come before Feature B. It cannot tell you whether either feature matters strategically. A roadmap can organize the next twelve months. It cannot tell you whether the company is building something competitors will eventually commoditize. And a vision statement can describe an attractive future without explaining why your company has any particular right to win there. That is why the strategy frameworks that remain useful tend to answer harder questions. Where should we compete? What is the actual problem standing between us and success? What will make customers choose us? What parts of our advantage will survive competition? And increasingly: If intelligence itself is becoming a commodity, what exactly does our product own? No single framework answers all of these questions well. The more useful approach is to understand what different strategy frameworks are designed to see, and equally importantly, what they are likely to miss. Here are five worth knowing. 1. Playing to Win A.G. Lafley and Roger L. Martin Playing to Win is probably the cleanest starting point for a product leader who has inherited something called a "strategy" that is actually a list of goals. Roger Martin's strategy choice cascade forces an organization to answer five connected questions: What is our winning aspiration? Where will we play? How will we win? What capabilities are required? And what management systems are needed to support those capabilities? The power of the framework is not any single question. It is the requirement that the answers fit together. Imagine a B2B software company saying: We want to become the leading AI platform for customer service. That sounds strategic. It isn't. Who is the customer? Large enterprises or small businesses? Customer-service leaders or IT departments? Are you competing on automation quality, implementation speed, compliance, integrations, cost, or something else? What does your product need to be unusually good at for that position to work? Playing to Win exposes this ambiguity. A strategy might become: We will serve regulated mid-market financial-services companies. We will win by providing AI customer-service automation that can be deployed without sending sensitive customer information into uncontrolled systems. To make this possible, we need unusually strong governance, integrations, evaluation infrastructure, and domain implementation expertise. Now we have choices. Where Playing to Win is strongest Its biggest contribution is forcing exclusion . Most weak strategies are additive. Serve enterprises. And SMBs. Build the platform. And applications. Sell directly. And through partners. Differentiate through product quality. And price. And service. And AI. Playing to Win makes this harder because "where to play" and "how to win" require actual choices. For product leaders, that discipline is valuable. Product organizations are naturally exposed to requests from sales, customers, executives, competitors, and engineering. Without strategic exclusions, the roadmap becomes the sum of those pressures. Where it falls short Playing to Win tells you to determine how you will win , but it does not automatically tell you whether the advantage you identify is durable. This distinction matters much more in software than it did a decade ago, and even more in AI. Suppose your answer is: We will win by providing the best AI-generated sales proposals. Good. But what if the models capable of generating those proposals improve every six months? What if Microsoft adds the capability to Office? What if Salesforce bundles it into its platform? What if every competitor has access to the same foundation model? You have made a strategic choice. You have not yet demonstrated strategic defensibility. Playing to Win is therefore an excellent choice framework , but it needs another lens underneath it to examine whether the chosen advantage can actually survive. 2. The Strategy Kernel Richard Rumelt Richard Rumelt approaches strategy from almost the opposite direction. Instead of beginning with aspiration, he begins with the problem. In Good Strategy/Bad Strategy , Rumelt argues for an action-oriented conception of strategy rather than treating goals, ambitions, slogans, or financial targets as strategy. His strategy kernel is commonly expressed through three connected elements: diagnosis, guiding policy, and coherent actions . That sounds almost trivial. It isn't. Consider a product company whose growth has slowed. The executive team might produce a strategy like: Increase enterprise ARR by 40%, improve retention, accelerate AI adoption, and become the market leader in our category. Rumelt would effectively ask: What is the problem? Maybe enterprise growth is not the problem. Perhaps the real issue is that implementation takes nine months. Or that buyers love the product but users don't adopt it. Or that the company wins departmental deals but cannot cross the security requirements necessary for enterprise-wide deployment. Those are completely different diagnoses. And therefore they demand completely different strategies. If implementation complexity is the constraint, the guiding policy might be to radically standardize deployment rather than expand product functionality. The resulting actions might include eliminating custom integrations, building migration tooling, narrowing supported configurations, and redesigning onboarding. Suddenly product strategy becomes coherent. Where Rumelt is strongest The Strategy Kernel is exceptionally good at forcing product leaders to distinguish between symptoms and constraints . That matters because product organizations frequently treat metrics as problems. "Retention is falling." That is a measurement. Why is it falling? "We need more enterprise customers." That is an objective. Why aren't enterprise customers buying? "We need better AI." Possibly. But what specific constraint would better AI remove? Rumelt's approach encourages a product leader to keep drilling until the organization has identified something causal enough to act upon. Where it falls short Diagnosis does not automatically create competitive positioning. Two competitors can correctly diagnose the same market problem and still require completely different strategies because of their assets, customers, capabilities, or distribution. The Strategy Kernel is therefore better at answering: What problem must we solve? than: Where should we compete? And it is even less explicit about another increasingly important issue: If we solve the problem, which part of the resulting value will actually belong to us? For that, product leaders need another kind of framework. 3. Supply Chain of Intelligence Anand Arivukkarasu AI creates an uncomfortable strategic problem. Many products can become dramatically better without the company that built them becoming dramatically more defensible. That distinction is easy to miss. A startup can integrate the latest foundation model, produce an impressive experience, grow rapidly, and still discover that most of its intelligence belongs to suppliers underneath it. That is the problem the Supply Chain of Intelligence , developed by product leader Anand Arivukkarasu , is attempting to address. The framework starts from a simple proposition: Intelligence is a supply chain, and value tends to accrue around bottlenecks. Rather than treating "AI" as one technological capability, the framework maps the system across multiple layers including resources, infrastructure, data, models, trust and gatekeeping, access, domain execution, orchestration, user surfaces, and memory. The current framework describes ten layers and fifty sublayers, while explicitly presenting the taxonomy as something that can evolve as the industry changes. This creates a very different strategic question from the earlier frameworks. Playing to Win asks: Where will we play and how will we win? Rumelt asks: What is the critical challenge we must overcome? Supply Chain of Intelligence asks: Where in the system does our company actually own something that cannot easily be removed, replaced, commoditized, or absorbed by another layer? That question is increasingly important. Consider a hypothetical AI recruiting product The company builds an excellent interface for recruiters. Underneath it: a third party provides the foundation model, another provider supplies embeddings, applicant data comes from existing systems, integrations provide workflow access, the model performs much of the reasoning, the interface packages the result. The product may be useful. But where is the company's leverage? If the foundation model provider improves its recruiting capabilities, does the startup become stronger or weaker? If the applicant-tracking system adds the same workflow, can the customer eliminate the product? If competitors access the same models, what compounds uniquely for this company? Perhaps the answer is proprietary hiring outcome data. Perhaps it is deeply embedded execution inside recruiter workflows. Perhaps it is accumulated organizational memory about what different hiring managers actually value. Perhaps it is a verification system customers trust. Or perhaps, after mapping the system honestly, there isn't much defensibility at all. That last possibility is precisely why the exercise matters. Where Supply Chain of Intelligence is strongest SCOI makes dependency part of product strategy. Traditional product thinking often evaluates a product looking outward: Customer → problem → product → competitor. AI products also need to be examined looking downward: Product → workflow → orchestration → model → data → infrastructure. A product can occupy a powerful customer position while simultaneously depending on an upstream supplier that captures increasing amounts of the underlying value. That creates strategic questions product leaders previously left mostly to engineering. Should we own the model? Probably not in many cases. Should we own the data? Maybe. Should we own verification? Should memory be product infrastructure rather than a feature? Should we build domain execution ourselves instead of simply orchestrating another provider? Where could the platform underneath us move upward? Where could the application above us move downward? Those are architecture questions, but they are also questions about bargaining power. SCOI is useful precisely because it connects the two. Its most valuable idea may be wrapper fragility "Wrapper" is sometimes used lazily as an insult against AI startups. That misses the point. Every software product wraps something. An application wraps operating systems, databases, cloud infrastructure, APIs, libraries, and increasingly models. The strategic issue is not whether you are a wrapper. The issue is: What remains uniquely yours after the wrapped component improves? That is a much more useful question. A thin interface around a model can become a substantial company if usage generates proprietary data, workflow ownership deepens, memory accumulates, trust compounds, and switching costs increase. Conversely, a technically sophisticated application can remain fragile if almost all of its customer value comes from components available equally to competitors. Where the framework should be treated carefully SCOI is also much newer than the other frameworks in this list. Playing to Win and Rumelt's work have been applied and debated across organizations for years. Wardley Mapping has developed a substantial practitioner community. DHM emerged from Gibson Biddle's experience including his product leadership work at Netflix. Supply Chain of Intelligence does not yet have that same history of independent validation. That matters. Its ten-layer taxonomy is useful, but users should resist assuming that because something has been placed into a framework it has therefore been proven. There is also a danger of false precision . A team can spend hours determining exactly which layer a capability belongs to while avoiding the much harder business question: Does anyone care enough about this capability to pay us? Architecture is not strategy by itself. Nor does owning a supposedly defensible layer guarantee success. A company can possess unique data and still lose because it has weak distribution. It can own customer memory and still build a bad product. It can control an important workflow but operate in a market too small to matter. SCOI is therefore best used as a defensibility and dependency map , not as a complete product strategy. That distinction actually makes it more useful. 4. Wardley Mapping Simon Wardley Wardley Mapping begins with an insight that sounds obvious but has profound strategic consequences: The components underlying a product do not remain equally differentiated forever. A Wardley Map combines a chain of user needs and dependencies with stages of evolution typically described as Genesis, Custom Built, Product, and Commodity . This gives product leaders something missing from many static strategy frameworks: movement. What is strategically valuable today may become infrastructure tomorrow. Think about cloud computing. There was a period when building sophisticated infrastructure capabilities could itself represent enormous differentiation. Eventually, large portions of infrastructure became something companies could simply rent. Similar transitions occurred with payments, communications, analytics, identity, search, storage, and countless other capabilities. AI is likely to accelerate this phenomenon. Something considered an impressive AI capability in 2024 or 2025 may be available through a low-cost API, open-source model, browser, productivity suite, or operating system shortly afterward. Wardley Mapping asks the product leader to think not only about where the company is positioned today, but where the underlying components are moving . Where Wardley Mapping is strongest It is particularly powerful for build-versus-buy decisions. If a component is rapidly commoditizing, building proprietary infrastructure around it may consume enormous resources while generating little future advantage. Conversely, a capability in an earlier stage of evolution may warrant experimentation and custom development. Wardley Maps can also reveal something psychologically difficult for product teams: Yesterday's differentiation can become tomorrow's plumbing. That is one of the defining strategic problems of AI product development. Where it falls short Mapping evolution is partly judgment. Two experienced leaders can disagree about where a capability sits on the evolution axis. And technologies do not always evolve in the clean, predictable manner implied by a map. More importantly, knowing that something is commoditizing doesn't automatically tell you what your company should build instead. Wardley Mapping shows terrain. It does not choose your destination. Its value therefore rises dramatically when combined with frameworks that address choice, diagnosis, or defensibility. 5. The DHM Model Gibson Biddle Gibson Biddle reduces product strategy to a deceptively compact question: How can the product delight customers in hard-to-copy, margin-enhancing ways? Those three dimensions form DHM: Delight, Hard to Copy, and Margin Enhancing. Biddle describes product strategy as hypotheses about how a company might accomplish those objectives, drawing heavily from his product experience at Netflix. The model is useful because product teams have a natural tendency to overweight the first dimension. Customer delight is visible. Customers ask for things. Design teams can demonstrate improved experiences. Usage metrics move. Product reviews improve. But a delightful feature that every competitor can reproduce next month may create very little durable economic value. DHM forces the second question: Is this hard to copy? Then comes the third: Does it improve the economics of the business? These filters are surprisingly powerful. Consider free overnight delivery Customers may love it. Delight: high. Hard to copy: perhaps low. Margin enhancing: possibly negative. Not obviously strategic. Now consider a recommendation system built from years of proprietary behavioral data. Delight: potentially high. Hard to copy: potentially high because competitors cannot instantly recreate the underlying data. Margin enhancing: potentially high if better recommendations increase retention or purchasing. That begins to look strategically interesting. Where DHM is strongest DHM connects product thinking with economics. That sounds basic, but product organizations often separate the two. One team discusses customer value. Another discusses technical differentiation. Finance discusses margin. DHM insists that strong product strategy should eventually connect all three. Where it falls short DHM works better as a test for strategic hypotheses than as a complete strategy-development process. Suppose a company identifies ten initiatives that delight customers, are difficult to copy, and improve margins. Which one should it pursue? Which market should it target? What is the central obstacle? Which capabilities are becoming commodities? Where does structural dependency exist? DHM doesn't fully answer those questions. And "hard to copy" deserves more scrutiny in the AI era. Something may appear hard to copy because it required twelve months of engineering. That does not mean a competitor will require twelve months next year. AI compresses reproduction costs. This is where DHM and frameworks such as Wardley Mapping or Supply Chain of Intelligence can complement one another. The mistake is trying to choose one framework Product leaders often ask which strategy framework is "best." That may be the wrong question. These five frameworks operate on different dimensions. Strategic question Useful framework Where will we compete and how will we win? Playing to Win What is the critical problem we actually need to solve? Strategy Kernel Where does defensibility and dependency sit across the AI system? Supply Chain of Intelligence Which underlying capabilities are evolving or commoditizing? Wardley Mapping Will this create customer value, defensibility, and better economics? DHM A sophisticated product strategy could therefore use all five sequentially. Start with Rumelt . Diagnose the actual strategic constraint. Then use Playing to Win . Choose where to compete and how you intend to win. Use Wardley Mapping to understand how the technological and competitive landscape underneath that choice may evolve. For an AI product, use Anand Arivukkarasu's Supply Chain of Intelligence to examine which parts of the intelligence system you control, which parts you rent, where suppliers have leverage over you, and where durable value might compound. Finally, use Gibson Biddle's DHM as a sanity check. Will the resulting strategy genuinely delight customers? Is some part of it difficult to replicate? And can it eventually produce attractive economics? A practical example Imagine you are the CPO of an AI sales-coaching startup. The obvious roadmap might include: better call transcription, more accurate summaries, automatic coaching recommendations, CRM integration, role-play agents, manager dashboards, personalized training. Those may all be good ideas. But they aren't yet a strategy. Rumelt First diagnose the constraint. Perhaps customers like AI coaching but frontline representatives don't use it consistently. The problem isn't coaching intelligence. The problem is adoption inside the workflow. Playing to Win You decide not to compete for every sales team. You focus on high-volume field-sales organizations where managers cannot physically coach hundreds of representatives. Your way to win becomes continuous, workflow-integrated coaching rather than generic conversational intelligence. Wardley Mapping You realize transcription, summarization, and generic role-play generation are rapidly becoming commodity capabilities. You should probably not build your strategy around being slightly better at them. Supply Chain of Intelligence You map the system. The foundation model is rented. Transcription is rented. Generic reasoning is increasingly available. But the company's customer-specific coaching data, observed rep behavior, manager feedback loops, domain execution, and longitudinal memory may compound with usage. Those areas deserve disproportionate investment. DHM Finally ask: Does deeply personalized coaching delight users? Possibly. Does accumulated organizational coaching memory become difficult to copy? Potentially. Could better coaching improve retention or reduce human management costs enough to support strong economics? If yes, now something resembling a coherent strategy has emerged. Notice what happened. The frameworks did not give the company an answer. They forced the company to ask better questions. That is what useful strategy frameworks actually do. What has changed for product leaders For a long time, product strategy could focus primarily on three things: customer, competitor, company. Those still matter. But AI adds another dimension: the supply of intelligence underneath the product. A product leader increasingly needs to understand not just customer behavior and product experience, but model capability, data advantage, inference economics, platform dependency, trust, orchestration, workflow ownership, and accumulated memory. That does not make the older strategy frameworks obsolete. It makes their boundaries more visible. Playing to Win remains excellent for choice. Rumelt remains excellent for diagnosis. Wardley remains powerful for technological evolution. DHM remains useful for testing whether product differentiation has economic substance. And Supply Chain of Intelligence introduces a useful additional lens for an era in which a meaningful portion of what makes a product "intelligent" may be supplied by someone else. The strongest product leaders will probably not become disciples of any one framework. They will know which question they are trying to answer before reaching for one. Because ultimately, a framework is not strategy. It is a way of seeing. And strategy improves when leaders can see the problem from more than one angle.

title: Google Gemini Adds Free Full-Length SAT Practice Tests With Instant Study Feedback
author: Ali Farhat
summary: Google Gemini now lets users take free, full-length SAT practice tests directly in the Gemini app . The feature combines vetted test content from education partners including The Princeton Review with immediate scoring, skill-area feedback, answer explanations, and a customizable study plan. It is a notable expansion of Gemini's education tools because it moves the product beyond on-demand question answering into a more structured test-preparation experience. Google says users can begin by prompting Gemini with a request such as “I want to take a practice SAT test.” According to Google's official Workspace update on Gemini SAT practice tests , the capability is available to Gemini users, including Google Workspace customers, Workspace Individual subscribers, and people using personal Google accounts signed into the app. For students, the central appeal is straightforward: a full exam can be accessed on demand at no cost, followed by feedback intended to identify where further study may be useful. For Google, the release shows how an AI assistant can be packaged around a repeatable learning workflow rather than used only as a general-purpose chatbot. A test-prep workflow inside Gemini The SAT feature is designed to mirror the experience of taking the real test through content that Google describes as vetted and sourced from partners such as The Princeton Review. Gemini then processes the completed practice test and returns results immediately. That matters because conventional practice-test workflows can separate the exam, scoring, review, and study planning into distinct steps or products. Google has described four connected elements of the Gemini experience: Full-length SAT practice tests that users can request on demand. No-cost access within Gemini. Immediate scoring and skill-area breakdowns after a test is completed. Answer explanations and a customizable study plan to support follow-up preparation. The company first announced the SAT capability in January 2026 and later included it in its student-focused Gemini feature overview. That overview also points to practice tests for JEE Main, while Google says more tests are planned. The stated direction is therefore broader than a single SAT tool, although Google has not provided a complete list of future exams in the supplied materials. Exam support in Gemini What Google has confirmed Content or follow-up support SAT Free, on-demand, full-length practice tests Vetted content from partners including The Princeton Review, plus scoring, skill breakdowns, explanations, and a study plan JEE Main Practice tests are included in Google's student-feature overview The supplied research does not specify equivalent content partnerships or test format details The distinction is important. Google has provided detailed SAT-specific information, including the role of The Princeton Review and the full-length format. Readers should not assume the same implementation details apply to JEE Main or future test categories until Google publishes them. Why vetted content changes the proposition Generative AI can explain concepts, create quizzes, and suggest revision plans. A full practice test introduces a different challenge: students need materials that are credible enough to use for exam preparation and structured enough to assess performance. Google's partnership-based approach addresses that concern by grounding the SAT experience in reliable source material rather than positioning Gemini as the sole author of the assessment. That does not make Gemini a replacement for official admissions guidance or every paid test-preparation service. The materials supplied by Google describe a practice and feedback experience, not an official SAT administration or admissions product. Still, the combination of a realistic test format, rapid results, and a study plan can reduce the friction between identifying a weakness and acting on it. Accessibility and the broader education strategy Making the feature free can broaden access to structured practice for students who already use Gemini through a personal account, Workspace, or Workspace Individual subscription. The practical benefit is not merely price. A student can initiate a test in the same conversational interface used for explanations and follow-up questions, potentially making review more immediate and less fragmented. The feature also illustrates a broader product pattern for AI assistants in education. Useful education AI increasingly depends on more than fluent responses. It needs reliable source material, a clear task flow, feedback that is understandable to learners, and boundaries around what the tool is actually designed to do. Google's SAT release brings those components together in a specific use case. For education providers, publishers, and tutoring businesses, this shift raises a strategic question: how will prospective students discover learning support as AI assistants become another entry point? A visible, well-explained offering in Gemini can matter alongside conventional search rankings, websites, and course marketplaces. As AI assistants become part of how students find academic support, education businesses need to understand whether their expertise is represented accurately in the answers those systems generate. Frequently Asked Questions Can Gemini provide free full-length SAT practice tests? Yes. Google has confirmed that Gemini offers on-demand, no-cost, full-length SAT practice tests. How do I start a SAT practice test in Gemini? Google says users can prompt Gemini with a request such as “I want to take a practice SAT test.” What feedback does Gemini provide after a practice SAT? After completion, Gemini provides immediate scoring, skill-area breakdowns, answer explanations, and a customizable study plan. Who provides the SAT practice content in Gemini? Google says the SAT experience starts with vetted content from education partners, notably The Princeton Review. Does Gemini offer practice tests for exams beyond the SAT? Google's student-feature overview also highlights JEE Main practice tests, and the company says more tests are planned. Conclusion Google's Gemini SAT feature turns a general AI assistant into a more structured study tool: students can take a full-length practice test, receive immediate feedback, and continue with a tailored plan in one place. Its use of vetted partner content is central to the release, while the inclusion of JEE Main and planned additional tests suggests that Google is building a wider exam-preparation capability within Gemini.
